# Coherent briefs and presentations

Build a shared argument spine: decision or problem → why it matters → evidence/diagnosis → strategic choice and rationale → customer and operating implications → economics → validation or next decision. Adapt order and depth to the audience. These are reasoning components, not mandatory headings or a fixed slide count.

## Brief

Lead with the thesis and what the reader should decide or understand. Give each section a distinct job. Connect claims with explicit reasoning; do not stack observations and call it strategy. Include credible alternatives, tradeoffs and uncertainties in proportion to their importance. Put research depth and detailed calculations in an appendix when they interrupt the executive argument. Compress repetition without erasing mechanisms or limitations.

Keep process narration, editing commentary and routine research qualifications out of executive copy. State observed findings directly at their supported scope. Keep decision-changing uncertainty next to the claim; put supporting methodology in notes or an appendix rather than repeating blanket caveats. Preserve customer-language promises and explain the mechanism and economic consequence behind them; neither a slogan alone nor an implementation inventory is a strategic narrative.

## Presentation

Determine whether it is for live discussion, a standalone read or a leave-behind from context; ask only if this changes the output and cannot be inferred. Design a narrative for that use. A discussion deck should leave room for questions; a standalone deck must contain enough explanation to make the logic self-sufficient.

Before adapting a brief, map its essential claims, customer paths and causal links to slides. Mark each as retained, combined, or intentionally omitted with a reason consistent with the user's scope. Use this as a compact working check, not extra executive copy. Shortening the deck must not silently remove an acquisition path, lifecycle stage or strategic distinction. Ensure the deck tells the same story without merely copying paragraphs.

Use takeaway titles and one primary claim per slide. Choose a visual that explains the relationship: journey, comparison, economics, dependency or decision. Icons must clarify meaning. Avoid decorative diagrams, redundant taglines, dense paragraphs and shrinking fonts to fit. Put supporting evidence and citations in readable footnotes or notes as appropriate; never hide decisive caveats. Apply requested brand assets and colors, while distinguishing a concept from an official company position.

Render and inspect every page/slide using the artifact skill. Verify hierarchy, legibility, overflow, clipping, consistency, accurate charts, source placement and reading order. A text-only review cannot certify visual quality. Recheck consistency between brief and deck, especially metrics, phase names and claims.

Also inspect communication: at presentation scale, can the reader identify the takeaway and the relationship without reading a paragraph or relying on the creator's explanation? For a journey, show meaningful connections and relevant branches/loops rather than isolated labeled boxes; do not add decorative connectors to unrelated content. Use a coherent icon system and custom iconography when requested. Cut text that the visual already explains. A clean, unclipped slide may still fail this test. Review rendered slides first, then compare their meaning with the source brief and coverage map.

## Prototype or interview support, only when requested

Make the prototype test or demonstrate one strategically important customer story, with the relevant employee/operating counterpart. Label simulated inputs and unimplemented capabilities; a persuasive demo is not proof of integration or economics. Do not build it just because AI makes it possible.

For interviews, adapt depth and how materials are introduced to the meeting's purpose and participants. Keep an outside-in point of view confident but provisional. Separate suggested questions from established facts about mandates, leaders and reporting lines. Use the latest supplied resume for personal claims, preserve qualifiers and avoid adding sensitive exact figures from memory.
